paras: The assault on a Black man in the Smithfield Red Shirt riot took place on July 31, 1900, at Smithfield, North Carolina, when an unnamed Black man in the crowd at a broken-up Populist speaking was "handled roughly" during a fight between Red Shirts and Populists. The incident was reported in a single sentence of a Raleigh dispatch to the New York Sun, which gave neither the man's name nor any injury. Other accounts of the Smithfield disorder, Democratic and Populist alike, did not mention him.

The riot came two days before the August 2 state election, in which North Carolina voters were to decide a franchise amendment that the Sun called the "anti-negro amendment." Senator Marion Butler had been scheduled to speak for the Populists at Smithfield but sent N. M. Teague in his place, while the Democrats held a rally the same day at which Solicitor E. W. Pou spoke. By the Sun's count about 5,000 people attended, many of them wearing red shirts and carrying rifles.

When Teague began to speak around noon, according to the Sun's dispatch, Red Shirts pulled the platform from under him and gave him five minutes to leave town. Friends of the Populists tried to push the Red Shirts aside, setting off a general fight in which sticks were used and two persons were cut. Directly after describing the Red Shirts running the Populists "out of sight," the dispatch added that "a solitary negro in the crowd was handled roughly," without saying who handled him, how, or why. The Red Shirts then returned and heard their own speakers out.

Later in the afternoon a crowd gathered at the office of J. D. Parker, the Republican editor of the Smithfield Courier, who telegraphed Governor Russell that his life was in danger. The governor ordered the Raleigh Light Infantry to Smithfield but cancelled the order after Sheriff J. T. Ellington wired that there was no need for troops.

No arrest, inquest or other official action concerning the Black man appears in the coverage. Parker's later statement, printed in the Sun and in the Populist Caucasian, described the beating of the legislative candidate Massey and other Populists and said a deputy sheriff standing within four feet did nothing, but it did not mention a Black victim.

The Sun ran the Smithfield story under the headline "Run Out by Red Shirts" and placed the assault on the Black man in passing, between the rout of the Populists and the resumption of the Democratic speaking. In a special dispatch headed "Not Called by Sheriff," the Democratic News and Observer of Raleigh blamed Republicans for disrupting Pou's meeting, described the burning of Butler in effigy as a "comic parade," and accused Parker of seeking "political capital"; it said nothing of a Black man. The Caucasian, a Populist paper at Clinton, headed Parker's statement "The Smithfield and Dunn Outrage" and called the Red Shirts "lawless," but it too was silent about him. No Black-press report of the incident was found.

Accounts of how the wider disorder began differed by party. The Sun's dispatch and Parker's statement said the Red Shirts attacked the Populist stand and beat and cut Populists, while the News and Observer said Republicans had cursed and threatened to break up Pou's meeting and that "a few determined red shirts" simply took Teague down and told him to leave. None of these versions addressed the Black man, whose treatment rests on the Sun's report alone.

bases: A crowd at a Red Shirt rally roughly handled a lone Black man during a general political fight, with no killing or threat to kill reported (A1).

accounts.label: Raleigh dispatch to the New York Sun
accounts.gist: Red Shirts pulled down Teague's platform, a general fight followed with two persons cut, and 'a solitary negro in the crowd was handled roughly.'

accounts.label: Republican editor J. D. Parker
accounts.gist: Red Shirts led by Abel beat Massey and other Populists, cut some with knives and pulled down the stand while a deputy sheriff looked on; no Black victim mentioned.

accounts.label: Democratic correspondent (News and Observer)
accounts.gist: Republicans disrupted Pou's meeting with profanity, and 'a few determined red shirts' took Teague down and told him to leave; no fighting or Black victim mentioned.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Run Out by Red Shirts' and 'Violence in North Carolina's Campaign' and noted the Black man in a single sentence between the rout of the Populists and the resumed speaking.
The News and Observer headlined 'Not Called by Sheriff', blamed Republicans for the disturbance, called the effigy burning a 'comic parade' and said Parker sought 'political capital'.
The Populist Caucasian headed Parker's statement 'The Smithfield and Dunn Outrage' and called the Red Shirts 'lawless'.

versions.value: Red Shirts pulled down the Populist platform; friends of the Populists pushed back and a general fight followed, with two persons cut
Red Shirts under Abel pulled Massey off the stand, kicked and beat him, and beat and cut other Populists
Republicans cursed and tried to break up Pou's meeting; a few red shirts took Teague down and he left

conflicts.note: The conflict concerns the wider riot; none of the accounts contradicts the Sun's sentence on the Black man, which only it reports.
